At the heart of every use of "skew" is a single idea: to pull something away from where it naturally, correctly, or straight-on belongs — making it tilted, lopsided, or distorted.

Whether something is physically crooked, data is thrown off balance, or an opinion is twisted, the word "skew" is capturing that same essential movement: away from straight, away from true, away from fair.

In its most concrete sense, to skew something means to cause it to sit or move at an angle instead of straight.

The strong wind skewed the satellite dish to one side.
The table legs are uneven, which skews the whole surface.

Here, you can almost picture something that should be perfectly upright or perfectly aligned — but instead it's been nudged, twisted, or pulled sideways. It doesn't have to be dramatic. Even a slight tilt counts as skewing.

It can also be used without an object, describing something that moves or sits at an angle on its own:

The car hit a patch of ice and skewed across the road.

In this case, nothing is doing the skewing to the car — the car itself is moving in a skewed, diagonal, uncontrolled direction.

This is where "skew" is used most heavily in modern English, especially in news, science, and everyday conversation about data.

To skew data or results means to distort them so they no longer give a fair, balanced, or accurate picture.

Imagine you want to find out the average salary at a company. Most employees earn $40,000–$60,000 a year. But the CEO earns $10,000,000. If you include the CEO's salary in your average, the final number will shoot up dramatically — giving the false impression that everyone earns a lot. That one extreme value has skewed the data upward.

The presence of a few billionaires in the survey skewed the average income figure dramatically.
Researchers removed the outliers because they were skewing the results.

The key insight here is that something — an unusual value, a biased sample, an unfair variable — is pulling the data away from what it would truthfully show, making it lean too far in one direction.

You'll often see the resulting form, "skewed," used as a describing word:

The data is heavily skewed toward younger respondents.
The skewed results made the drug appear more effective than it actually was.

When data is skewed, it is not wrong in a simple, obvious way — it's leaning. It's telling a partial truth that misrepresents the whole picture.

"Skew" extends naturally beyond data to describe how any kind of perception, judgment, account, or understanding can be distorted or biased.

Growing up wealthy can skew your understanding of how difficult everyday life is for most people.
The documentary was criticised for skewing the facts to support its argument.
His deep love for the team clearly skews his judgment when evaluating their performance.

In each of these cases, something is being tilted away from objectivity, balance, or truth. A person's background skews their worldview. A filmmaker's agenda skews the story. A fan's emotions skew their analysis.

This is perhaps the subtlest but most powerful use of the word, because it acknowledges that distortion doesn't have to be intentional or dishonest — sometimes life experience, emotion, or circumstance quietly pushes our perception sideways without us even noticing.

An important and useful feature of "skew" is that it almost always implies a direction — something isn't just distorted randomly, it's distorted toward something or away from something.

Skewed toward the wealthy — meaning it benefits or favors wealthy people more.
Skewed toward pessimism — meaning someone tends to see things more negatively than is accurate.
Skewed to the right (in statistics) — meaning the data has a long tail stretching toward higher values.

This directional quality is what makes "skew" so precise and useful. It doesn't just say "this is wrong" — it says "this is leaning this way, and that lean is the problem."

The reason "skew" works so well across all these situations is that the underlying image is always the same: something straight, balanced, or true has been pushed off-center. Whether it's a physical object, a set of numbers, or a person's perspective, skewing means that what you're seeing is no longer a fair, straight-on view of reality — it's been angled, and that angle matters.

If you ever encounter this word and feel unsure, ask yourself: What should be straight or balanced here? And in which direction has it been pulled away from that? Answer those two questions, and you'll have fully understood what "skew" is doing in that sentence.
